newsitem.title: GERMANY: German roaster aims for higher Polish coffee sales.
newsitem.headline: German roaster aims for higher Polish coffee sales.

text.p: German coffee roaster J.J. Darboven aimed to raise sales of roasted coffee to Poland to 200 tonnes a month in 1997 from 120 tonnes at present from its own local plant, plus 20 tonnes per month of direct imports, it said.

Export manager Cornelis de Groot said in an interview the Polish coffee market may grow by 15 percent next year, citing rising purchasing power in the wake of economic growth and a successful fight against inflation.
"Polish coffee consumption is growing and will offer good earnings for those growing with the market," he said.
Apart from groceries, Darboven specialises in supplying hotels and restaurants, where it offers professional coffee-makers and accessories along with the product.
De Groot said Poland, where consumption has risen five-fold since 1989, had become the most promising coffee nation in the former east bloc.
Polish consumers would become richer faster than other countries in the region because of a high percentage of owner-occupied homes and commercial companies.

Poles attached high value to coffee, which had become an alternative currency in communist days, but they also simply enjoyed drinking it, while other tea-drinking nations in eastern Europe still clung to that habit.
Darboven, which in 1993 entered into a joint venture with roaster Rumia near Gdynia, bought the company in 1994.

It produces two robusta-intensive brands, Santos and Colombiana for the local market, but also sells its German flagship product, Idee, an easily digestible coffee which has aggressive agents removed in a patented physical process.
The local brands must have seven percent of grain added to keep value added tax to seven percent rather than 22 percent payable on pure roasted coffee, de Groot said.
Imports of ready roasted coffee incur an 18.3 percent tax plus three percent border tax, which encouraged local production.

But Polish coffee-drinkers paid no less for coffee than their western European neighbours as dollar-denominated raw materials costs were the same and inflation and retailers' margins cancelled out the effect of lower labour costs. --Vera Eckert, Hamburg newsroom, +49-40-41903275
